4. **Parent/runtime owner:** integrate shared writes once, run the affected combined checks/build, publish immutable artifact identity, bind/freeze/launch via the maintained operation, then accept recovery. Parent should not become a fourth author of every family’s detailed fixtures and caller. During control-only execution, an already isolated next-family scout may proceed under an explicit non-timing policy; timed measurements retain global quiet.

These bounds are planning/review targets grounded in the observed 5–10minute source slices and 10minute caller preparation, not promised throughput. If two workers need the same shared file, use staged patches against one agreed preimage and one parent integration; do not let nine family agents mutate a shared certificate/catalog/selection service. Keep only one or two prepared candidates ahead of the client so obsolete artifact bindings do not accumulate.

Track assignment→complete prepared slice, prepared slice→candidate, candidate→control outcome, and client attempts caused by contract mismatch in the existing milestone. Do not add another dashboard or require timing bookkeeping before a port. A lower source-to-client queue and fewer parent repair turns would demonstrate improvement; worker count would not.

## 1. Consume cloud color only on eligible translucent pixels

**Observed source:** `program/c1_blend_layers.fsh:430–442` reads
`read_clouds_and_aurora` before checking `is_translucent || is_translucent_lod`.
Only that branch consumes the color. The helper at
`include/sky/clouds/sampling.glsl:5–24` fetches pixel age, gathers apparent
distance, reads filtered color with explicit LOD, and conditionally samples
lightning scattering.

**Experiment:** keep apparent-distance gather and the lightning implicit-LOD
sample in their original control-flow context initially. Defer pixel-age
`texelFetch` and cloud-color `textureLod` until the existing translucency
predicate succeeds. Preserve the original filter LOD, returned alpha/color,
refracted coordinates and both vanilla/DH flags. Do not change deferred terrain
clouds or rainbow behavior in this first arm.

**Work potentially avoided:** two logical texture operations plus filter-age
arithmetic on opaque composite1 pixels. This is distance-independent consumer
dispatch, not another cloud-distance budget. It can help the adapter's total
cost, but does not by itself prove shader LOD.

**Risks:** the compiler may already avoid discarded reads; a new varying branch
may add divergence. GLSL 4.10 §3.8.2 and §8.9 constrain non-uniform control flow
and implicit derivatives. Moving implicit-LOD operations requires verified
sampler state or gradients computed before divergence; a clean compile alone
does not establish correctness. [Khronos GLSL 4.10 specification](https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/gl/GLSLangSpec.4.10.pdf).

**Acceptance:** static output/consumer inspection, then actual Iris rendering
with glass, ordinary water, DH water, lightning and overlapping near clouds.
Inspect motion/disocclusion and history resets. Require unchanged visible
compositing and a repeated composite1/whole-render improvement; if timing is
flat, retain the negative result and stop extending the guard.

## 2. Skip fog shadow reads outside the shadow-map domain

**Observed source:** `include/fog/overworld/raymarched.glsl:113–165` evaluates
distorted shadow coordinates and reads shadow depth every fog step. The colored
path reads two depths and shadow color before its outside-domain fallback;
the non-colored path reads one depth before multiplying comparison depth by an
in-domain flag. Fog density, extinction and scattering remain meaningful there.

**Experiment:** place only the shadow texture reads behind a valid-domain
predicate and use the intended fully-lit fog-shadow value outside it. Preserve
all in-domain lookup math and all density/integration steps. Test this alone,
with the existing original step count, before any fog sample adaptation.

**Work potentially avoided:** one shadow fetch per outside-domain sample on
the current non-colored profile, or three on colored-shaft variants. Far DH
rays may offer more qualifying samples; that coverage is a prediction requiring
a diagnostic capture. Surface shadow filtering is unchanged.

**Risks:** out-of-range `texelFetch` cannot establish reference parity. At a
normalized coordinate of exactly one, the integer texel can equal texture size.
The coordinator must choose and document a half-open valid texel domain or an
explicit edge rule. This is a correctness-sensitive boundary change, not a
promise of bit identity to invalid original reads. Domain divergence and
per-step predicates can cost more than the saved reads.

Spatially coherent conditions are preferable to random neighboring branches in
the general SIMD model. GPU Gems 2 §34.1/§34.2.4 explains that mechanism on old
NVIDIA hardware; it does not quantify M3 behavior. Apple's current M3 Metal
heat-map documentation independently separates control-flow divergence from
instruction cost. [GPU Flow-Control Idioms](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems2/part-iv-general-purpose-computation-gpus-primer/chapter-34-gpu-flow-control-idioms),
[Apple performance heat maps](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/analyzing-apple-gpu-performance-using-performance-heatmaps-a17-m3).

**Acceptance:** original and guarded arms with matched fog counts, normal and
elevated cameras, shadow-map edges, sunrise/night, rain, colored shafts, DH
present/absent and moving camera. Compare fog transmittance/scattering and
map-edge continuity separately from GPU time. Reject visible light-shaft loss.

## 3. Dispatch constant sky AO output immediately after combined depth

**Observed source:** `program/d3_ao.fsh:95–134` reads combined depth, then reads
Gbuffer and two noise texels, optionally classifies vanilla/DH depths, reconstructs
positions and reprojects history. For `depth == 1.0` it writes constant ambient
and history-data outputs and returns. None of that preceding work is consumed
by the sky output.

**Experiment:** move the exact existing sky output/return directly after
combined-depth fetch. Retain the terrain AO algorithm, original constants and
hand logic. Never replace combined depth with vanilla depth; DH terrain must
reach the terrain branch.

**Work potentially avoided:** three logical fetches and reconstruction/history

This is another structural dispatch cleanup rather than distance-quality LOD.
AO is already half resolution, limiting its likely whole-frame contribution.

**Risks:** driver optimization may already sink the reads; early exits affect

reads before moving the return. Do not assume output parity merely because sky

## 4. Test whether transition noise destroys sample-budget coherence

**Observed source:** local `lod.glsl:88–123` rotates per-pixel interleaved gradient
noise and uses it to select tiers within transition bands. Far/near stable
regions already bypass noise in `shaderlod_quality_at`. Cloud budgets can use
march noise, so tier selection and primary ray jitter may currently share an
input. Upstream cumulus primary steps vary with ray direction, density skips
lighting, and transmittance terminates the march: uniform tier selection alone
does not imply uniform execution.

**Experiment:** cloud-only diagnostic prototype, original ray jitter unchanged.
Separate tier-selection noise from ray-sample jitter. Compare original per-pixel
tier noise with a noise value shared by each 2×2 group of cloud-pass texels,
keeping per-pixel distance tests, probability thresholds, budgets and temporal
sequence advancing. Start with 2×2 only; no new classify pass, subgroup
instructions or persistent history cache. First show that transition bands
occupy enough pixels to matter. Near/far constant regions are the control.

**Work potentially avoided:** no guaranteed reduction in selected scalar samples.
The hypothesis is reduced mixed-budget execution within SIMD groups and less
inactive-lane work in transition regions. Group layout is unknown on the
OpenGL driver; 2×2 image groups do not prove SIMD alignment.

**Risks:** shared randomness preserves marginal tier probabilities only under
a suitable sequence; it changes spatial correlation and can create visible
blocks or low-frequency flicker. Screen-fixed groups can swim under camera

error spectra matter; it supports the quality test, not this coarse-noise
optimization. [Wolfe et al., Scalar Spatiotemporal Blue Noise Masks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09629),
especially the spatial/temporal analysis and volumetric application.

**Acceptance:** offline tier distribution and budget fixtures over distances and
frame phases; debug transition coverage in a separate unmeasured run; real
cloud jitter/history unchanged. Inspect slow camera motion, horizon pans,
camera translation and cloud/weather motion at ordinary upscale 4 and premium
upscale 1. Require stable cloud structure without blocks/rings, then paired
cloud-pass and whole-render gains. Do not report an offline lane model as M3
performance evidence. Preserve this as default-off if any visual cost is found.

## 5. Replace fixed SSR stepping with bounded pixel-space DDA research

**Observed source:** `include/misc/raytracer.glsl:31–78` normalizes a screen-space
direction, computes a boundary length, divides it by intersection step count,
and fetches one depth per step until hit/exit. Refinement fetches occur at
`:88–105`. A fixed count can revisit texels on short projected rays or skip
thin geometry on long rays. The current source does not record their frequency.

**Experiment:** first record/replay projected rays and integer depth-fetch
coordinates without changing the rendering algorithm. If duplicate visits are
common, prototype a separate Photon-only raytracer using perspective-correct
pixel-space DDA with original fallback color/composition. Start DH absent,
stride 1, bounded original maximum work and careful depth/thickness conversion.
Only after its quality/cost is understood test a modest larger stride on far,
rough surfaces, keeping glossy water conservative.

McGuire and Mara §3/Listings 2–4 describe contiguous pixel traversal, depth
interval tests, clipping and stride/jitter controls. They recommend coarse
stride for rough surfaces and explicitly show its artifacts. Their 2014 GPU
timings cannot predict this host. [Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing](https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf).

**Work potentially avoided:** redundant depth reads on short projected rays;
later coarse stride can reduce visits on qualifying far/rough surfaces. DDA can
instead visit more pixels than Photon's original budget, and requires extra
setup/interval math. Never claim fewer steps from its name alone.

**Risks:** changed hit semantics/thickness, self-intersections, hand clipping,
thin reflections, grazing water and screen edges. A camera-distance threshold
alone does not establish reflection-error tolerance. DH depth/projection
selection is a separate extension, and current DH+SSR sampler limits remain.
This experiment must not become a sampler-allocation pass split implicitly.

**Acceptance:** synthetic depth/ray fixtures plus actual no-DH SSR rendering;
near glossy water, far rough metals, thin poles, screen-edge rays, sunlit/night
and moving reflections. Compare hit masks and visible reflections against both
original SSR and a higher-sample reference, then repeated GPU/frame costs.
Promote distance stride only if motion quality survives and it beats a simple
existing lower-SSR-quality control at comparable fidelity.

## Measurement and stopping rules

The project's asynchronous elapsed queries measure a completion interval, not
isolated ALU occupancy. CPU command starvation, driver scheduling and tiling
can affect it. Khronos ARB_timer_query revision 13 §5.4, Issues 5/8/10 and its
example discussion specify completion timing, variance, tile-order caveats and
the cost of waiting for same-frame results. Keep delayed nonblocking reads;
do not add glFinish or nested elapsed queries. [ARB_timer_query specification](https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/extensions/ARB/ARB_timer_query.txt).

Apple documents source-level cost/divergence tools for **Metal** on M3. No
successful Metal capture of this Iris/OpenGL path was established by this
research. Do not make direct Metal tooling a prerequisite, or label existing
elapsed timers hardware shader-occupancy counters.

For each arm, use one GPU client, identical window/resolution/pacing and shader
inputs, warmed chunks/histories, exact archive hashes/effective options, and
separate quality captures. Compare pinned original, candidate disabled and
candidate active without changing optional-mod stack or terrain radius. Start
with a small balanced repeated pilot before a long matrix. Existing attribution
scopes may overlap; do not sum their medians as total frame cost.

Prefer same-JVM controls where a compile-time switch is unnecessary, and retain
balanced serial archive controls to expose reload/JVM drift. Runtime reload
may reset histories, so warm up each arm. Match measured wetness, world age and
biome inputs; leave actual frameCounter advancing. Static animation/wetness
diagnostics must remain explicitly identified and followed by normal-motion
quality checks. See [GPU_TIMING.md](GPU_TIMING.md) and
[IN_PROCESS_RESULTS.md](IN_PROCESS_RESULTS.md).

First accept driver compilation/rendering, then visible parity or an explicit
quality budget, then repeatable affected-pass and whole-render improvement.
A pass gain with unchanged total frame time is effect evidence with a practical
bottleneck limit. It is not the shared project's ordinary-scene ≥15% acceptance
gate. Require its ordinary-scene plus second-workload evidence independently.
The compiler can eliminate apparent source work, so logical fetch counts are
upper-bound hypotheses rather than issued GPU operation counts.

## Returned decisions and practical next step

The coordinator should request a concrete shader-file handoff from the protocol
owner for the isolated composite1 cloud guard, or assign its implementation to
that owner. This research agent retains no shader/GPU ownership. Compile/render
that arm with original sample budgets, then run matched forest and coastal pilots
and inspect glass/DH water/lightning before extending it into deferred terrain.

Fog-domain edge behavior needs an explicit correctness decision. Coarse tier
noise and SSR traversal need their own exploratory quality tolerance, not a
silent change to protected defaults. Stop the three structural candidates after
flat qualified pilots; prioritize the remaining experiments only when actual
transition coverage or duplicate SSR texel visits supports the premise.

# Iris-mandatory Vulkan path, current source check

Checked 2026-10-07, completed 13:25 PDT. Owner: `iris_vulkan_path`.
Read-only research except this report and ignored public-source receipts.
Root owns strategy, source integration and the client/GPU. No GPU lane was used.

## Decision

**No accessible, executable Iris Vulkan shader-pack route for native Minecraft
26.2/26.3 was established.** Keep the successful OpenGL ports and their explicit
backend refusal. Do not relax that refusal or benchmark a vanilla Vulkan boot as
ShaderLOD support. The upstream development premise is real: the Iris organization
publishes Aperture documentation and a current Slang example pack. However,
Aperture is a different pack pipeline, and its engine, loader/version metadata,
license and executable Mac artifact were not available from the checked public
endpoints. This is an access/API prerequisite, not proof that the project does
not exist or that future Vulkan support is impossible.

A separate public Iris-derived Vulkan fork was found and inspected. Its concrete
pipeline placeholders rule it out as an immediate rendering prerequisite. It
targets Fabric 1.21.1 and custom VulkanMod rather than Mojang's native 26.x backend.

The user requires Iris and authorizes modifying/forking it. Root must resolve
whether an Iris-team successor satisfies that requirement; do not silently rename
Aperture as a compatible Iris fork. Engine Git ancestry is unavailable here.

## Current primary-source evidence and pins

All raw HTTP responses, timestamps and SHA-256 receipts are under
[`dev/upstream/iris-vulkan-r1`](../dev/upstream/iris-vulkan-r1/receipts.json), which
is ignored by Git. Fresh checked endpoints:

- [Official Iris organization inventory](https://api.github.com/orgs/IrisShaders/repos?per_page=100):
  public `docs` and `Aperture-Example-Pack` are present. No Aperture engine appears
  in this response. `IrisShaders/Aperture` API returned HTTP 404 again; this cannot
  distinguish private from absent. [Modrinth Aperture project lookup](https://api.modrinth.com/v2/project/aperture)
  also returned 404, which only describes this particular slug.
- [Official Iris branch inventory](https://api.github.com/repos/IrisShaders/Iris/branches?per_page=100):
  current 26.2 commit `f61d950f556f3962d0e2e29c270bc1865572b35d` and 26.3 commit
  `770155cc91d8c11272d93cb4457fac1625d37a4d` remain the previously examined commits;
  no named Vulkan branch appears in this inventory. Do not infer absence of
  private work. Public 26.3 source still declares 1.11.6, not exact released
  1.11.7 ancestry.
- [Publisher Iris versions](https://api.modrinth.com/v2/project/iris/version):
  current 26.3 artifacts are 1.11.7, both loaders. The 1.11.0+26.2 Fabric release
  explicitly states Vulkan is unsupported. Current publication availability
  does not prove a new backend.

### Aperture public interface

Pinned official documentation commit:
`98f84cbe456e7e367afe788885869be46681be8c`.
The [migration guide](https://github.com/IrisShaders/docs/blob/98f84cbe456e7e367afe788885869be46681be8c/src/content/docs/aperture/migration.mdx)
warns its GLSL instructions are extremely outdated and Aperture has moved to
Slang. Treat that old guide as architectural context only. It describes explicit
pipeline construction rather than the implicit Iris/OptiFine graph, changed
texture/uniform interfaces and cascaded shadows; existing private GLSL patches
cannot be presumed to load unchanged.

Pinned official [Slang example](https://github.com/IrisShaders/Aperture-Example-Pack/tree/0e4816dce559ac7d6f00092fab190eae1178e2af)
commit `0e4816dce559ac7d6f00092fab190eae1178e2af`, current default branch `slang`:

- `shaders/pack.ts`: `configureRenderer`, `configurePipeline`, explicit
  screen-sized `mainTexture`/`finalTexture`, BASIC and SKY_TEXTURES objects,
  POST_RENDER gamma composite, combination pass, `beginFrame(WorldState)`.
- `objects/basic.slang`: imports `aperture`, uses `Vertex`, `vertexMain` and
  `fragmentMain`, `SV_Position`/`SV_Target0`, `ap.world` values and built-in
  albedo/lightmap sampling. No equivalent legacy pack entrypoint is established.
- `iris.d.ts`: declared texture dimensions, compile-time `exportInt`/`exportFloat`,
  command-list state, streaming buffers with explicit uploads, camera/projection/
  frame state. These suggest possible budget and uniform delivery seams, but
  declarations alone establish neither actual Java hooks nor resource lifetimes.

The repository description permits use of the example; the GitHub license field
is null and no license file appears in its pinned tree. Preserve attribution;
do not infer an Aperture engine license from the example or current Iris LGPL.
The example intentionally omits shadows, buffers and compute tutorials. No
Photon/Complementary port or compatibility artifact was discovered in this
bounded official inventory. It is not itself an executable shader engine.

### Shipped Iris binaries, both loaders

Independently disassembled existing exact JARs using private JDK 25 `javap -c -p`.
[`binary-audit.json`](../dev/upstream/iris-vulkan-r1/binary-audit.json) records
paths, SHA-256 and complete compiler/backend disassembly:

| Target | Fabric SHA-256 | NeoForge SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Iris 1.11.4 / 26.2 | `f1f7ab57c974d193ba33aa285864a0ded949216f402116fceaf4dc7739b4dd7c` | `5faeb646ff117bfc29e636baa9085f6fff6d048a328618749a991fd01c70019d` |
| Iris 1.11.7 / 26.3 | `83ab4d3013dd56ac05ae503a2f596968911001c4ef3d82c59c5c79e64c34dd98` | `2260506334a17ac566ea30169ab491201208f55c1c7212bb987bc0c7c59a8d93` |

Each observed `IrisRenderSystem.getGlDevice()` casts the actual backend to
`GlDevice`. Each `GlShader` calls OpenGL shader creation/compilation and each
`ProgramCreator` calls OpenGL linking. In 26.3 those are Renderpearl OpenGL
classes. Thus the exact released 1.11.7 binaries close the earlier source-version
ambiguity for this specific backend fact. Their full source ancestry remains
unresolved. No Vulkan-named entries were found in these JAR inventories; that
negative search is supporting evidence, not the decisive fact.

## Native Vulkan and Mac requirements

[Mojang 26.2 documentation](https://www.minecraft.net/en-us/article/minecraft-java-edition-26-2)
specifies Vulkan 1.2 plus dynamic rendering and push descriptors, with MoltenVK
translation to Metal on macOS. It documents backend preferences with fallback
and the actual backend shown in F3. A preference alone cannot certify Vulkan.

Actual 26.3 client binary inspection confirms:

- `PreferredGraphicsApi` contains DEFAULT, OPENGL and VULKAN; serialized names
  `default`, `opengl`, `vulkan`.
- VULKAN tries `VulkanBackend` then `GlBackend`; DEFAULT and OPENGL try GL first
  then Vulkan. This is observed 26.3 behavior, not inferred from 26.2 defaults.
- `Options.preferredGraphicsBackend()` is persisted under
  `preferredGraphicsBackend` and its tooltip reports restart required when the
  selection differs from startup. Therefore a second ShaderLOD backend selector
  is unnecessary for initial selection and cannot safely be treated as a live
  shader reload toggle.
- `DeviceInfo` exposes `backendName`, driver, features, limits, extensions,
  depth convention and timestamp period. `FrontendGpuDevice` exposes managed
  textures/views/buffers. Existing ShaderLOD 26.3 observation uses this API;
  its Apply gate allows only observed OpenGL. Its GL uniform/driver hooks must
  remain excluded from any future Vulkan path.

[MoltenVK runtime guidance](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/MoltenVK/blob/fae55a18779ee59da2cc5373a367a0282779c171/Docs/MoltenVK_Runtime_UserGuide.md)
is pinned to `fae55a18779ee59da2cc5373a367a0282779c171`. It lists macOS 12 minimum
for that upstream runtime, the required extensions and portability constraints.
MoltenVK converts SPIR-V to Metal shaders; Vulkan feature availability does not
guarantee every pack format/operation is available or faster. The bundled game
MoltenVK version and actual M3 Max enabled capabilities were not measured here.
Do not replace the game's bundled native library merely to match this upstream
guide. A system Vulkan SDK installation is not established as necessary.

## Public Iris-derived fork: concrete exclusion

[trptrk/Iris-Vulkan](https://github.com/trptrk/Iris-Vulkan/tree/9bae8e9a3c8b6ec34f871657b36331ebcd9f1a84)
at `9bae8e9a3c8b6ec34f871657b36331ebcd9f1a84` forks
`aaaapai/Iris-Vulkan-Port`. Both expose LGPL-3.0 metadata and no releases in the
checked release endpoints. Source declares MC **1.21.1**, Fabric 0.16.5,
VulkanMod-specific classes and a custom VulkanMod 0.5.9 compile input. Mod ID is
`iris-vulkan`, depends on VulkanMod, and conflicts with stock Iris and Sodium.
It is not an official Iris-team fork or a native 26.x backend port.

The inspected code contains real SPIR-V compilation logic, but
`IrisGraphicsPipeline.getHandle()` explicitly returns a zero placeholder;
`createShaderModules()` comments out the actual module creation and only marks
the modules created. These are executable missing implementations, not merely
stale comments. Therefore compilation/boot logs there cannot establish an actual
Iris shader render. The compiler comment also says Vulkan 1.2 while the active
shaderc target enum selects 1.1; do not copy its stated requirements blindly.
No build or launch of this fork is warranted before the missing draw path is
implemented and its substantial native 26.x migration is accepted by root.

## Next decisive experiment and implementation ownership

Preferred upstream route needs **accessible pinned Aperture engine source or
artifact, explicit license, actual loader/game/dependency targets, Mac native
requirements and one compatible real requested pack**. Root must resolve Iris
identity semantics. Once those exist, one owner should run a single original
pack on actual Vulkan, prove backend + current pack pipeline + native viewport +
decoded scene pixels, then implement/pin budget delivery and compare Off → On →
Off at matched native choices. Example-pack rendering can qualify the engine
only; it cannot satisfy Photon or another requested pack. A Vulkan API name
predicts no FPS gain, especially through Metal translation.

If literal Iris is required and Aperture cannot qualify, modifying the public
LGPL Iris source is authorized, but this is a real backend implementation:
compiler/SPIR-V interface layouts, managed render graph/attachments, uniform
buffers/descriptors, shadows, compute, temporal resources, Sodium coupling and
resize/reload/destruction must work together. Removing `GlDevice` casts or
adding a no-op backend class does not advance rendered support. Do not launch a
long retry against existing GL-only binaries.

Useful finite work meanwhile: continue actual shared shader cost reductions on
the existing GL renderer; reuse the pure preset/work-budget and reversible source
ownership decisions. An explicit pack-native pipeline budget can later port to
Slang/TypeScript after an actual upstream graph is available. Preserve the GL
downloads; use separate build variants initially if Aperture dependencies and
mixins conflict, deciding consolidation from real metadata rather than guessing.

Conditional next worker ownership once upstream source is accessible:
`ports/26.3/{fabric,neoforge}/.../integration/RendererBackend.java` for certified
backend observation; version-specific uniform/completion mixins only after exact
upstream hook inspection; a separate explicit Aperture pack adapter resource for
one requested compatible source, with its original/On/Off test. Existing pack
transaction service remains one separately owned integration seam. No proposed
Java Aperture class names or injection selectors can be certified from public
TypeScript declarations alone. Root must partition these files before assignment.

## Checks and boundaries

Actually run: bounded official metadata/source HTTP fetches; pinned source and
license inspection; four exact local Iris compiler/backend binary disassemblies;
26.3 client enum/options/backend/device API disassembly; inspection of the public
Iris-derived fork's compiler and actual placeholder pipeline; read current
ShaderLOD backend policies and uniform/completion hooks. The first binary command
used a wrong `ProgramCreator` package and failed; corrected exact class inspection
completed all four artifacts. That read-only failure remains in tool history.

No builds, tests, shader compilation, clients, GPU runs, encoders, SSH/Windows
actions, upstream messages or production edits occurred. All short fetch/javap
processes finished; this worker owns no live process. This report proves source
readiness boundaries only, not Vulkan rendering, visual quality or performance.

# Mac DH bottleneck diagnosis — 2026-10-25

CPU2 has a real, conditional CPU benefit on this Mac. Installing DH does not stop it from executing. More pixel work and DH rendering reduce its effect on total-frame throughput. This is diagnostic evidence, not a qualified ShaderLOD master-Off → On gain or a Windows result.

CPU2 means `quad_command_compaction` plus its required `shadow_admission_cache`. The controlled comparisons leave the master switch On, using zero optimization requests as the native control. Normal CPU-only Apply preserves the pack/pipeline identities and reload count. This isolates the optimization from master-switch reloads. Neither component was tested individually.

Apple M3 Max; NeoForge 21.1.253 / Minecraft 1.21.1; pinned local Iris 1.8.12 and Sodium 0.6.13; native MakeUp 9.5g and BSL 10.1.8. Fixed coast pose, RD12, day7000/clear, private server simulation frozen, native quality and AA. DH3.3.3 installed only in the middle phase, public DISABLED/DEFAULT renderer state, radius128, distant generation disabled. Shader animation clocks remain native, so this is not a fully deterministic workload. Two actual advertised fullscreen resolutions:1920×1200 and2560×1600; the latter has78% more pixels.

Low-overhead normal frame clocks and detailed CPU/GPU profiling ran in separate windows. Frame CPU is GameRenderer render-thread CPU; frame interval includes the rest of the loop/presentation. Fine CPU scopes were sampled every16frames and repeated invocations aggregated per sampled frame. GPU queries sampled every16frames with category rotation. GPU elapsed is command-timeline duration, not utilization or pure shader execution; zero-valued small scopes do not establish zero cost. CPU/GPU scopes overlap and must not be added.

The middle client used two counterbalanced windows per state/resolution. Values below use equal-window mean frame times; displayed FPS is their reciprocal. The native control has all optimization requests Off, with the master switch On in both columns.

| Resolution / DH renderer | No requests FPS | CPU2 FPS | Observed FPS delta | Render CPU saved | Total frame saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1920×1200 / Off | 254.2 | 281.5 | +10.7% | 0.406ms | 0.381ms |
| 1920×1200 / On | 189.6 | 199.8 | +5.4% | 0.789ms | 0.268ms |
| 2560×1600 / Off | 191.1 | 194.1 | +1.6% | 0.327ms | 0.083ms |
| 2560×1600 / On | 139.3 | 141.6 | +1.6% | 0.664ms | 0.115ms |

Window p95 intervals at1920/DHOff improve4.88–4.92→4.55–4.59ms. At1920/DHOn they are6.28–6.33→6.34–6.40ms: the mean FPS improvement does not improve p95. High-resolution p95 ranges overlap. Full distributions remain in the raw exports.

The ~1.6% high-resolution deltas are within observed variation; they are not established gains. At2560/DHOn, render CPU falls4.545→3.881ms while the frame falls only7.177→7.062ms. This is direct evidence that less CPU work need not improve throughput proportionately. Resolution sensitivity supports a graphics/pixel-work limit; no hardware busy counter was collected.

The first DH-absent bracket averaged +4.6% but varied strongly (native239–276FPS, CPU2255–285). The return bracket gave native243–255 versus CPU2270–282, an equal-window +10.7% observation. Do not pool sessions or promote one bracket as a universal gain. The installed-disabled result is compatible with the absent return; there is no demonstrated installation-only suppression.

Consumption is established: all14 retained CPU2 performance windows remove54.35–54.45% of eligible command entries, with zero invalid compaction metadata and zero increase in the native full-validation counter across those windows. The profiled native GL submission wrappers execute34world+16shadow calls/frame with and without CPU2. Compaction reduces entries within those existing multi-draw calls, preserving the geometry; it does not remove half the GL calls or shaded pixels. Example paired profile observations show world submission CPU1.156→0.567ms, while command assembly stays small/slightly increases. These sampled wrapper durations include observer cost and drift; they are attribution evidence, not standalone speed qualification.

DH-disabled observations have DISTANT_HORIZONS absent, no additional actual DH draw calls, drained render-loading/chunk-conversion queues, and named DH worker CPU totaling roughly0.008–0.009core-equivalents (under1% of one core). File-handler maintenance continues. This does not support background DH work as the major bottleneck in those measured windows. The independent pinned-source audit shows why disabled rendering can still admit background work; it does not imply that such work was heavy here.

With DH enabled, the main MakeUp matrix executes117opaque+109translucent DH draws/frame. Separate profiles put the two DH render API paths together at about1.06–1.08ms render-thread CPU/frame, unaffected materially by CPU2. Main-path GPU elapsed observations are about1.77–2.16ms. These intervals include integration and submission effects and do not isolate DH shader arithmetic. The direct DH_DRAW timer category yielded no scopes on this route; outer API timing and actual draw/index counters are the available DH evidence. Do not treat the missing category as no GPU work.

BSL, master Off, also slows with DH:183.6→116.4FPS at1920 and124.2→84.1FPS at2560. These are single diagnostic pairs, not repeated optimization tests. Its DH paths cost about1.20ms CPU in the profile, with main/deferred GPU elapsed observations1.74/0.22ms. This supports a DH render/integration cost across both tested families, not a MakeUp-only failure.

Important rejected/inconclusive evidence remains visible. Three128→64→128 radius windows had queued loading and changing draw counts during measurement; none supports a distance-performance claim. Master-Off → master-On/no-requests → master-Off controls gave246.1→248.3→214.3FPS, despite unchanged native option maps. That return drift prevents a reliable original-relative suite gain. Earlier failed attempts include unsupported monitor mode, readiness/focus setup failures and a highly unstable capture; they are retained separately. A load average above80 was observed during early setup, but no causal attribution of the frame-time drift to host load, clocks, reload state or animation is established. Detailed DH profiles also drifted relative to the earlier FPS windows; do not combine them to inflate gains.

The next engineering priority should be benchmark reliability and isolation of the DH render/integration path before another optimization. Keep general shader performance in scope: CPU2 helps with DH absent, and installing DH is not the failure mechanism. DH is a measured high-cost workload worth prioritizing, but these two Mac packs do not justify a DH-only product. For PC, rerun the same stable-pipeline control with the current build, prove executed work, and attribute CPU/GPU costs before explaining the5080 discrepancy. Lower driver submission cost or another limiting stage is a hypothesis, not a measured PC finding.

Carry forward these benchmark requirements: same-pipeline feature toggles where possible; separate explicit master/mod-absent overhead controls; repeated and counterbalanced returns; native options/AA and active-work fingerprints; settled DH queues and stable geometry before accepting a cell; separate low-overhead performance and detailed profiling; observer calibration; explicit native animation state; rejected/noisy results reported alongside successes. A focused deterministic animation-phase experiment and driver/reload investigation remain needed to explain the master-control drift.

Added development-only, opt-in frame-boundary CPU/GPU recording controls, sparse CPU layers and a request-driven bottleneck probe. Default timing behavior remains unchanged. `compileDevClientJava`, `ManualProfilingGateTest`, `SparseGpuTimerGateTest` and `CpuTimersTest` passed. This work does not implement another optimization or qualify the other shader adapters.

The three completed client phases used 29.1minutes including boot, warm-up, control operations and recovery: 431seconds of captured frame intervals plus 213seconds of separate profiling. Earlier rejected attempts and instrumentation/setup repair add preparation time. Setup/mode/focus repairs and repeated client warm-up were the main delay. Final runs collected42performance windows and15profiles; three radius windows are excluded, while noisy master controls remain explicitly inconclusive. All27 configuration/archive preimages were restored byte-for-byte; temporary inputs removed; all clients and owned supervisors released. No PC work, commits or pushes.

Evidence: [summary](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/summary.json), [full analysis](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/analysis.json), [absent](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/a_absent_r5/results.json), [installed](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/b_installed/results.json), [return/master controls](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/c_absent_return/results.json), [source audit](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/source-audit/findings.md), [restoration](../../dev/logs/mac-dh-bottleneck-diagnosis-20261025-r1/restoration.json). Per-phase directories contain launch plan, operator source, raw samples, profiles, guard receipts and exact release evidence. Raw artifacts remain outside Git.

# Settings compile activation independent source review

**Scoped source acceptance: no blocking regression found.** The normal settings
forward path now performs the existing post-load compile activation using the
same selection transaction. This addresses the R46 Quality→Performance shape
where requested depth remained true while the newly selected private option
loaded0. Actual Java build/tests and the R47 runtime transition remain parent
acceptance; none were run by this reviewer. No client/GPU or source edits.

Inspected handback:
`dev/logs/performance-readiness-20261016/settings-bootstrap-r47-9okihkii/source-handback.json`.
Independently rehashed both main files and both focused test files; all four
still equal that receipt. Main SHA values are ShaderLodSettings
`7cebc515ee1b82e2ae9d6cff0d05fbcd9a895717c2acce6fac948eb0ae4ed288`
and CompileOptionControl
`698929a24af680ec7a3a19c31551500064d5caa608588beeea0199962e2607c0`.

## Target state and transaction ownership

Public ShaderLodSettings captures native renderer eligibility before suspension,
then keeps its existing selection.prepare and previous-settings preimages.
It writes/saves the requested enabled/preset before calling the new forward

## Current reuse and the forced shadow traversal

Sodium already avoids rebuilding a clean visibility graph. In
`SodiumWorldRenderer.setupTerrain`, lines 197–207 compare exact camera position,
pitch/yaw, fog distance and projection matrix. A change marks the graph dirty.
The update loop at lines 223–240 calls `RenderSectionManager.update` only if
`needsUpdate()` is true. Manager update builds lists then clears
`needsGraphUpdate` (`RenderSectionManager.java:131–136`). Thus unchanged-camera
static-world reuse exists upstream; a blanket "cache visibility" feature
would duplicate it.

However, the pinned Iris shadow path forces a traversal even when those
ordinary inputs are unchanged:

1. `ShadowRenderer.renderShadows` calls `LevelRenderer.needsUpdate()` before
   shadow terrain setup, bytecode offset 399.
2. Sodium's `LevelRendererMixin.java:113–116` injects at that method's RETURN
   and calls `SodiumWorldRenderer.scheduleTerrainUpdate()`.
3. That method marks its manager dirty (`SodiumWorldRenderer.java:144–149`).
4. Shadow setup then reaches the ordinary update loop. Iris's
   `iris$forceChunkGraphRebuildInShadowPass` also rebuilds when interpolated
   sun angle changes, otherwise returns the manager's dirty flag.
5. Iris's `cancelIfShadow` injects **after** `createTerrainRenderList` inside
   manager update, not at its HEAD. It returns before
   `needsGraphUpdate=false`. The shadow traversal has happened, and the dirty
   flag intentionally remains set for the later main traversal.

Consequently the shared flag is not safely "cleared too early" by shadows;
Iris explicitly preserves it. The unconditional dirtying plus preservation
can force both shadow and main traversals. Count the actual producer chain
before calling it waste: part of the behavior maintains shared mutable lists.
Iris's sun-angle gate alone cannot defeat the unconditional mark. The separate
`iris$forceEndGraphRebuild` makes the shadow update loop stop after one pass.

Iris already maintains separate outer `shadowRenderLists` and `shadowTaskLists`
in `MixinRenderSectionManagerShadow`. Its redirects cover list/task writes in
creation/reset, render-layer/list/count reads and task submission. It cancels
`updateChunks` and `uploadChunks` at HEAD while shadows are active. The vanilla
LevelRenderer save/restore mixin swaps its vanilla visible sections and camera
rotations; it does not snapshot Sodium's entire state.

## The hidden ownership problem: inner lists are shared

Separate outer lists are insufficient for reuse:

- `RenderRegion.java:46,60,209–210` owns one persistent `ChunkRenderList` and
  returns it from `getRenderList()`.
- `VisibleChunkCollector.java:43–53` obtains that object, resets it for the
  current traversal generation, adds section membership, and stores the same
  reference in its outer list.
- `createRenderLists` sorts those same objects (`VisibleChunkCollector.java:74–113`).
- `SortedRenderLists.java:14–17` merely stores an array of those references;
  it does not deep-copy section arrays.
- No inspected pinned Iris mixin separates the region's inner list. The JAR's
  Sodium region mixin concerns arenas rather than this list ownership.

A main traversal can therefore overwrite the membership/order/counts inside
an older shadow outer container, and a shadow traversal can mutate objects
referenced by a main container. Reusing one outer list after the other phase
has run is not an immutable snapshot. This is a concrete reason not to cancel
the force-dirty call or skip `setupTerrain` based solely on camera/sun equality.

## Safe narrow prerequisite: separate per-region inner lists

The ownership API needed for a default-off no-skip prototype is small:

| API / source | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `new ChunkRenderList(RenderRegion)` / lines 30–32 | Public constructor, ordinary Java arrays; no GL resource allocation |
| `reset(int frame)` / lines 34–40 | Resets geometry/sprite/entity counters and size; stores traversal generation |
| `add(RenderSection)` / lines 80–98 | Appends local section IDs according to current flags |
| `sortSections(SectionPos,int[])` / lines 46–77 | Reorders geometry membership by camera-relative region distance |
| `sectionsWithGeometryIterator`, sprite/entity iterators | Consumers of mutable membership arrays/counts |
| `RenderRegion.getRenderList()` / lines 209–210 | Single bounded substitution point for phase ownership |

Retain the original region list for the main phase. Lazily create one additional
list owned by the same region for the shadow phase, return it only when the
explicit feature/Photon eligibility cache and Iris shadow phase are active.
Keep all traversals, graph dirtying, generation increments, queue cleanup,
build scheduling and uploads unchanged. No cache skipping is authorized by
this prerequisite. Disabling must return the original getter behavior; the
existing forced traversals repopulate containers on each following phase.

Each list owns three `byte[256]` membership arrays: 768 raw bytes plus object
and array headers/counters. A typical compressed-reference HotSpot layout is
roughly 0.85–1 KiB additional heap per shadow-visited region, not a measured
host size. Region lifetime owns the extra list; avoid a static map that retains
unloaded regions. Lazy construction avoids paying for regions never used by
shadows. The getter adds cached feature/phase branches; construction is once
per region, not once per frame. Sorting already allocates a small histogram
per list (18 ints for the pinned 8×4×8 region shape); this prototype does not
remove that cost or promise faster frames.

Actual consumer checks are still required. In particular
`tickVisibleRenders()` reads main `renderLists` to activate animated sprites
(`RenderSectionManager.java:252–275`), and the inspected Iris shadow redirects
do not include that method. Shared-array mutation currently affects what it
sees during shadow setup. Isolation must inventory and deliberately preserve
the required sprite activation for both visible main surfaces and animated
shadow casters rather than silently dropping one set. Test counts/order and
animations; do not claim list isolation alone is perfectly behavior-neutral.

Direct Sodium types require the exact pinned Sodium compile-only artifact in
main compilation; existing runtime dependencies do not imply its classes are
already on the main compile classpath. Keep the production dependency policy
consistent with Iris's mandatory Sodium runtime.

## Dirty producer and consumer inventory

| Input/producer | Existing action | Required reuse treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manager creation/reload/world replacement | Manager starts dirty; old sections/resources destroyed | Bind all cache state to manager + world identity; never transfer it |
| Exact camera position/orientation/projection/fog change | Public `markGraphDirty`, world-renderer lines 197–207 | Separate phase keys; preserve original numeric comparisons and camera-relative transform |
| `LevelRenderer.needsUpdate`, explicit terrain update | Public mark chain above | Record reason; only suppress the precisely identified redundant shadow force after prerequisites |
| Section add/remove | Direct true writes, manager lines 213/240 | Invalidate both phase memberships, neighbor topology and queued work |
| Rebuild scheduled | Pending update promoted and direct true write, lines 598–615 | Task collection and geometry epoch; graph cannot be frozen while a build is pending |
| Build outputs uploaded | OR graph dirty with `processChunkBuildResults`, lines 295–308 | Both phases see changed built state/flags/connectivity/global entities |
| Section info update | `setRenderState` compares built/flags/visibility, `RenderSection.java:150–165` | Preserve selective dirtying; ordinary mesh/index updates still flow through region storage |
| Sort tasks/results and camera movement | `processGFNIMovement`, `scheduleSort`, upload integration | Preserve separate sort/task epochs; not every sort sets the graph-dirty flag |
| Spectator/solid origin, smart cull | `shouldUseOcclusionCulling`, manager lines 165–176 | Exact effective mode belongs in traversal key |
| Search/render radius | `getSearchDistance`, manager lines 153–162; radius reload in setup | Per-phase effective search radius and renderer identity |
| Iris sun/light/frustum/pipeline settings | Sun gate, new frustum creation, shadow range/settings | Exact generated plane/box/projection key and pipeline generation |
| DH frustum/projection presence | Shadow-frustum source can use DH projection | Optional DH readiness/projection belongs in shadow key; DH lists remain independently owned |

Iris disables Sodium fog occlusion while a shader pack is present in
`MixinRenderSectionManager.iris$disableFogOcclusion`; a changed fog distance
can still dirty ordinary setup. That suggests a possible redundant-key
component, but removing it alone without phase ownership/other producers
cannot establish safe reuse.

Manager `lastUpdatedFrame` increments per traversal, not per game frame.
`OcclusionCuller` uses that stamp plus each section's incoming-direction state
to avoid repeat visits. `RenderSection.lastVisibleFrame` is shared across
phases; `RenderSectionManager.isSectionVisible` compares it to the current
manager stamp (lines 282–292). Collector lists also carry that stamp. World
entity culling, rebuild submit/upload stamps and sprite activity consume related
state. A cached draw-list pointer does not preserve all those generations.

## A viable later reuse design requires additional work

After isolated inner lists are validated, introduce an explicit structural
dirty epoch bumped by **all** existing graph producers, including direct field
writes and relevant build-result updates. Each phase records its consumed epoch
and exact traversal-input key. World and shadow consumption must not erase
the other phase's invalidation. Reusing visibility can only replace the
graph search/list construction, never the whole terrain setup routine.

Separately retain/recollect pending task queues, sort triggers, section frame
membership and sprite/entity consumers. An initially simpler cache can reuse
only shadow visibility while main keeps its normal updates, provided shadow
memberships are isolated and every relevant structural/key producer invalidates
them. Even this requires the shared traversal-stamp consumers to be modeled;
an old generation cannot be mistaken for current main visibility.

No source-only proof currently establishes complete epochs for that change.
The next actionable step is **instrumentation without skipping**:

1. Count shadow force-dirty calls, other public marks, direct add/remove/rebuild
   writes, graph-changing uploads, phase traversal calls and consumed epochs.
   Attribute the exact force call without broad stack walking in the hot path.
2. Record phase camera/frustum/search/mode fingerprints, region/section list
   identities, ordered local membership hashes and collector generation stamps.
   Compare the same region's lists before/after the other phase to prove aliasing.
3. Add default-off inner-list ownership separation only; compare unchanged
   main/shadow identities, counts, order, animated sprites, task progress and
   render outputs during movement, loading/unloading, edits and shader/world
   reloads. Measure its memory/branch overhead independently.
4. Only after every producer/consumer is covered, consider reusing graph
   search for exact unchanged keys. Differential visibility/caster checks and
   frame timings must decide whether it has useful benefit.

A changed vanilla/DH detail radius reduces the work by changing visible detail;
it remains an existing geometry-quality knob. Correctly avoiding a repeated
identical traversal would be a distinct optimization preserving the same
section/caster set, but this audit does not claim that result has been achieved.
There is no safe one-line head cancellation identified here.

# Evaluation

## Setup evidence

| Check | Required evidence | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NeoForge skeleton | Successful build/test command and output artifact | Java and build setup |
| Runtime dependencies | Pinned versions, artifact sources and hashes | Reproducible dependency selection |
| Client startup | Launch command and runtime log | Loader/mod startup |
| Photon under Iris | Selected pack, successful compilation and in-world scene | Working shader runtime on recorded hardware |
| DH installed | Mod loaded and actual distant terrain in a scene | DH render integration |
| DH absent | Iris/Photon client renders without DH | Optional dependency behavior |
| Initial LOD | Disabled/enabled comparison plus near/far/transition inspection | Observable first distance LOD behavior |
| Agent setup | Parse profiles/config, execute hook, validate local skill | Local infrastructure correctness |

A shader parser or lint pass is useful but does not substitute for shader
compilation on the Minecraft OpenGL driver. Report partial checks explicitly.
A setup pass need not prove the entire later optimization hypothesis.

## Performance proof

Use a repeatable scene with a fixed seed/save, coordinates, camera direction,
time/weather, resolution, render distance, resource pack, and Photon preset.
Record Minecraft/NeoForge/Iris/Sodium/DH versions, Photon revision and patch,
GPU, driver, OS, Java, mod config, and every relevant shader option.

Warm up chunk loading, shader compilation, temporal effects, and GPU clocks.
Compare the same patched pack with LOD disabled versus enabled so unrelated
upstream changes do not enter the result. Keep DH absent for the first normal
terrain optimization proof; test DH as a separate compatibility/extension run.
Use repeated windows or interleaved runs to expose noise and drift.

Measure GPU frame time when tooling on that hardware permits it, with per-pass
or capture evidence for the modified effect. Record median and tail behavior,
measurement method, sample duration, and variability. FPS may diagnose total
frame behavior but is insufficient to attribute a GPU optimization. CPU/chunk
loading bottlenecks can hide the result.

Before the first performance decision, record the acceptance criterion with the
user in `docs/DECISIONS.md`. The illustrative 8 ms to 6 ms example in the idea
outline is a motivating example, not a frozen requirement. If gains are within
noise, investigate whether branching or changed samples actually reduce work
before adding more packaging.

## Visual and compatibility checks

Inspect near objects, transition bands, distant geometry, thin geometry,
reflections, water, moving camera, temporal accumulation, and hard material
boundaries for the effect changed. Capture the baseline and LOD view from the
same camera. Include debug LOD colors when useful; a debug overlay itself does
not prove that an expensive effect changes its workload.

For the MVP, expand to DH terrain/water and the vanilla/DH depth boundary,
shader reloads, config reloads, unsupported Photon versions, Iris absence,
DH absence, and renderer version mismatches. Only promote a component set to
supported after its runtime behavior has been checked.

Keep raw logs/captures/worlds outside Git and link reproducible local paths or
summarized reports from the active goal. Never label a planned check as passed.

# Native-resolution in-process effect control

`benchmarkFeature=effects` adds an explicit four-phase global Iris bridge
control with the five Photon effect options held constant. It accepts all-active,
mixed or all-off effect maps. Each phase changes only `lod.enabled`; it does not
reload the shader pack or alter a module option. The existing default `global`
mode still requires all five modules off, and `coherence` still controls only
the original-Photon shadow coherence flag with global enable held true.

This is dev-only source integration, not shader support or performance evidence.
The runtime coordinator owns compilation and all client/GPU launches. No main
config, uniform transport, shader source or adapter was changed for this mode.

## Runtime setup and evidence

Use a frozen no-atmosphere Photon archive and prepared profile with the same
native framebuffer, camera/save, upstream quality, detailed/DH radii, runtime
artifacts, sampling cadence and pacing as the experiment being investigated.
The existing Gradle mappings accept these properties:

- `-PgpuBenchmark=true -PbenchmarkOnly=true -PbenchmarkFeature=effects` selects
  the new control and exits after the report/images complete.
- `-PbenchmarkStartEnabled=false` selects OFF/ON/OFF/ON; `true` reverses the order
  to ON/OFF/ON/OFF. Keep separate immutable output profiles/reports for each run.
- `-PbenchmarkSettleSeconds=...` supplies the existing between-phase warmup.
  Initial warmup, measurement duration, GPU/CPU controls, fixed wetness and
  `benchmarkWindowScale` use their existing mappings. Actual captured framebuffer
  dimensions remain authoritative; scale alone does not establish resolution.

Workload capture and benchmark capture are mutually exclusive. The session
preserves previous reports, records unique session/phase UUIDs, retains phase
images/hashes, and restores the initial global enable and HUD state on completion
or failure. A source check rejects the Photon lighting atmosphere guard before
the first effects phase and exports `atmosphere_guard_absent=true` only after
that check passes. The report method is distinct:

> One JVM/world/pipeline; fixed five-module effect options; only live global bridge enabled changes

At each boundary, the runtime requires actual ShaderLOD presence, a live Iris
pipeline without fallback, a hidden HUD, and the expected global enable value.
Terrain policy, culling, visibility lists and coherence must all be unconfigured
and inactive. Loaded semantic config remains identical except enable; debug,
cached sky and analytic water are false, and preserve-lighting/use-mod-config
are true. All five `SHADERLOD_CLOUDS`, `SHADERLOD_WATER`, `SHADERLOD_FOG`,
`SHADERLOD_SSR` and `SHADERLOD_MATERIALS` options must exist with literal string
values `true` or `false`. A module flag being true does not prove its underlying
upstream feature is enabled or its work survives compilation.

The existing boundary and tick checks preserve the archive hash, complete
effective option map, semantic config, camera/world inputs and world/pipeline
object identity throughout the four phases. GPU backend/sample epochs, source
frame ranges, timing policies and fixed wetness supplier observations keep their
existing checks. The report hashes loaded artifacts and bounded development
directory trees; changes to those frozen files during a run remain forbidden.
Window telemetry is retained with its sampled-state limitations.

## Analysis and acceptance

```sh
python3 scripts/analyze_inprocess_control.py PROFILE/benchmark.json \
  --expected-shader-sha256 EXACT_ARCHIVE_SHA256 --profile PROFILE \
  --output dev/logs/EXPERIMENT/effects-inprocess-analysis.json
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_inprocess_control.py
```

The analyzer accepts active effect flags only when `benchmark_feature` and the
instrumentation feature explicitly say `effects`, the method matches, the
selected flag is `lod.enabled`, and the atmosphere guard check is recorded as
passed. It rejects missing/nonliteral effect flags, unintended option/config
changes, CPU feature activity, malformed identities, shader/archive changes,
timing epoch reuse, image/temporal failures and incorrect phase alternation.
Complete effective option maps and runtime artifacts must match across compared
sessions. A different archive is recorded as a separate source intervention;
it does not imply a particular code path caused a difference.

Report phase timings and the two adjacent ON-versus-OFF contrasts separately
from same-state drift. These are four correlated phases in one JVM, not four
independent JVM replicates; no frame-derived confidence interval or independent
run statistics apply. Reverse-order controls help inspect drift but do not
establish a universal gain. GPU intervals, CPU wall/thread clocks and derived
frame duration remain separate. Window unknowns remain unknown. The pipeline
identity check is a declared runtime source check; exported raw object IDs and
runtime linked-uniform readback are unavailable.

The native nine-arm pilot did not identify a module as the cause of the active
regression. Original/global-off were approximately 61 FPS; all-active and
all-off were approximately 56 and 55 FPS in separate JVMs. Keep those retained
results and failures. This new control holds a single compiled pack/world/JVM
steady while checking whether the global bridge changes timings with fixed
effect options. It is a diagnostic, not a correction to that pilot's result.

Tool acceptance is 20 lightweight Python fixtures, including all nine existing
global/coherence fixtures, forward/reverse effects controls, malformed/missing
flags, option and semantic drift, bridge/lighting protections, artifact/session
differences, timing-free controls and static Java routing/method checks. No Java
compiler or client was run by this file owner. The coordinator must compile the
integrated dev sources, then retain successful or failed native four-phase runs
and inspect screenshots before drawing runtime/performance conclusions.

Iris's complete loaded option map can also contain incidental pass/header

settings controls plus explicit user overrides. Unrequested non-settings default
entries are listed under `omitted_non_settings_defaults`; they retain each
archive's source declaration and are not silently reclassified as user knobs.

# Headless development on the Asahi host

The host runs without SDDM or the Plasma desktop. Minecraft still needs a display
server. `shaderlod-display.service` supplies a private KWin virtual output and
Xwayland, using the Apple M1 GPU at 2560×1600, scale 1. It does not depend on the
physical panel or lid state. This is a different presentation backend from the
old desktop; do not pool its timing results with old desktop measurements.

The service uses its own D-Bus session and configuration under
`~/.local/share/shaderlod-display/`. It does not load the Plasma workspace or
change personal desktop settings. Its environment file is private, lives under
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/shaderlod-display/`, and is checked against the current service
invocation. Readiness rejects software GL rendering and incorrect resolution.

## Normal use

Use the commands in [the benchmark guide](BENCHMARK.md). On Linux ARM64,
`run_benchmark.py test`, `check`, and `native-startup` automatically start and
select the installed headless service if neither DISPLAY nor WAYLAND_DISPLAY is
set. `plan`, discovery, report, build, and recovery do not start it. An explicitly
selected desktop display takes precedence.

For interactive development launches, use `scripts/linux_arm64_runtime.py client
on|off` with the ordinary `dev_client.py` arguments. This also selects the
headless display. Direct Gradle or `dev_client.py` launches need a suitable
display environment; they do not automatically select one. A virtual display
does not provide remote viewing by itself. Benchmark still captures remain
available in the report directory.

```sh
python3 scripts/headless_display.py --wait
systemctl --user status shaderlod-display.service
journalctl --user -u shaderlod-display.service
```

Stop the service only after all owned Minecraft clients have exited:

```sh
systemctl --user stop shaderlod-display.service
```

The next maintained launch starts it again. The installed user service is enabled
at login-manager startup, with user lingering enabled for this host. It is
independent of T3 and network services. No reboot is needed to restart it.

## Installation and recovery

The checked-in unit assumes the checkout is `~/ShaderLOD`. Back up any existing
unit before installing, and adjust its script path if the checkout moves:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user ~/.local/share/shaderlod-display/config ~/.local/share/shaderlod-display/data
cp scripts/systemd/shaderlod-display.service ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now shaderlod-display.service
```

Dependencies are the existing `kwin_wayland`, Xwayland, `dbus-run-session`,
`glxinfo`, `xrandr`, Python 3 and user systemd installation. Native Java, Iris and
shader requirements remain unchanged. Do not substitute Xvfb/software rendering
for performance testing.

`shaderlod-lid.service` holds logind's low-level `handle-lid-switch` inhibitor.
This overrides the base `HandleLidSwitch=suspend` setting: logind takes no action
on lid events while the service holds the lock, on battery or external power.
It is enabled independently of the display and T3, using the existing lingering
user manager, and needs no administrator credential. The base system policy is
unchanged. Verify the live lock with `systemd-inhibit --list` and the enabled
service with `systemctl --user is-enabled shaderlod-lid.service`. Stopping that
service restores the base lid behavior. It does not block explicit suspend or
protect against an exhausted battery.

Install the lid service (back up an existing unit before replacement):

```sh
cp scripts/systemd/shaderlod-lid.service ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now shaderlod-lid.service
systemd-inhibit --list
```

To return to the full desktop, stop the headless service with no client running,
then enable/start `sddm.service` with administrator privileges. Preserve network
and T3 startup configuration. The local backup and validation evidence for the
headless transition is in `dev/experiments/headless-development-20261103/`.

## P1 — 26.1.2/26.2 Apply can mutate and reload an unsupported backend

Exact primary locations:

- [26.2 Fabric Apply](../ports/26.2/fabric/src/main/java/com/pp/shaderlod/fabric/FabricLodSettings.java#L22):
  prepare at line 24, config replace at 27, forward reload at 29; generic failure
  restores/persists config at 40 and attempts another reload at 45.
- [26.2 NeoForge Apply](../ports/26.2/neoforge/src/main/java/com/pp/shaderlod/ShaderLodSettings.java#L17):
  prepare at 19, config mutation/save at 23–25, reload at 26; generic failure
  saves at 39 and reloads again at 49.
- Corresponding 26.1.2 Fabric and NeoForge settings files have the same ordering
  and lack any backend preflight.
- [26.2 guard](../ports/26.2/fabric/src/main/java/com/pp/shaderlod/integration/RendererBackend.java#L11)
  throws `IllegalStateException`; the core mixin only invokes it at uniform
  registration TAIL (Fabric line 37, NeoForge line 39). 26.1.2 behaves likewise.

Source counterexample: with a functioning settings screen and selected pinned
Photon, change enabled/preset while the actual backend is unsupported. Apply
does not call the backend guard before `selection.prepare`. The shared
[transaction](../src/main/java/com/pp/shaderlod/integration/PackSelectionTransaction.java#L98)
calls `runtimeFacts()` only for the two pinned AstraLex sources, so Photon skips
that check entirely. Preparation can generate/select a private archive and save
Iris config; the loader then persists its config and calls `Iris.reload()`.
If core registration reaches the guard, failure is an ordinary exception rather
than a recognized refusal, leading to restoration and a second unsafe reload.
If Iris internally catches shader construction failure, its fallback status also
leads into that same generic recovery path. Thus refusal is too late regardless
of whether upstream ultimately throws or enters fallback.

The AstraLex path does not provide a general backend gate either:
[currentIrisFacts](../ports/26.2/fabric/src/main/java/com/pp/shaderlod/integration/KnownRuntimeBoundary.java#L65)
catches the guard's RuntimeException at 71, returns partial facts, and the known
crash matcher rules out its historical 1.21.1 tuple when the current Minecraft
version differs. GL driver reads themselves are correctly downstream of the
guard; that protection does not prevent Apply mutation/reload.

This is a reproducible source control-flow defect; no unsupported-backend client
was launched. Vulkan may fail earlier inside Iris, which can make the UI path
unreachable on a particular stack but does not establish safe ShaderLOD refusal.
26.1.2's vanilla renderer is OpenGL; alternative/unknown backends still remain
outside the certified boundary. Severity reflects unsafe-case acceptance, not a
demonstrated OpenGL crash.

Suggested fix: carry 26.3's `requireApplySupported()` before transaction creation,
using a dedicated recognized refusal that returns without config writes, pack
preparation, restoration or reload. A meaningful gate should count **zero**
backend selects/saves, config writes and reloads on refusal through actual public
Apply, rather than only testing pure backend-name eligibility.
